title: Save the planet, change your diet
summary: NH gives non-ideological tips for a sustainable, healthy diet that apply whatever you eat: buy local and seasonal, prefer whole foods, avoid overbuying and food waste, shop with a plan and a list, use small specialized stores, cut takeout, and cook for yourself. He also stresses eating meals with others and eating foods you enjoy, which saves money and improves your relationship with food.
claims: Diet is overrated for muscle building compared with programming, but underrated for sustainability and long healthy life
Sustainable eating isn't about going vegan or carnivore; dietary tribalism misses easier measures everyone can apply
Focus on improving your local environment and community rather than an abstract 'planet'
Buy local: fresher, often better quality and price, lower transport footprint, and it builds community ties
Support small businesses where possible, or big corporations end up with no competition
Buy seasonal produce: cheaper, less transport, more variety, and you discover new favorite foods
Minimize processed food; choose the least-processed versions, e.g. bread from a mill without added sugar
Buy animal products directly from the source rather than processed meat products with added sauces and sodium
Whole foods are cheaper than processed food; a head of cabbage costs about 28 cents and feeds you for two days
Don't overbuy perishables; only stock up on non-perishables and buy what you'll eat so nothing gets thrown away
Go grocery shopping after a meal so hunger doesn't drive extra purchases
A French study found about 30% of food bought by households is thrown away
Food waste is the biggest diet-related environmental problem
Shop with a list; without one you'll overbuy, since supermarket music and layouts are designed to trigger impulse purchases
Plan the week's meals and cooking so impulse buys have no room in your schedule
Supermarkets pair products like coffee and sugary foods to trigger cravings; small specialized stores avoid this
Cut takeout: it pollutes, costs about five times more than cooking, and restaurants load food with butter, sugar and sodium
Men who never learn to cook stay in a state of infancy, moving from mom's cooking to takeout
The vast majority of what you eat should be whole foods you cook yourself; restaurants are fine occasionally
Make meals a social ritual; eating with others is good for mental health
People who eat with family or friends tend to have fewer eating disorders, which are lonely illnesses
There are no foods everyone must eat and few truly bad ones; eat what you like and try many foods
Following these tips can save a few hundred to about $1,000 a year and improve your relationship with food and micronutrient intake
